# [A]{.k-a2} — Annotated {#annotated}

::: {.tada-key}
**Annotation** is adding comments **within each code file** — denoted with `#`
in R and Python — or embedding code within an **RMarkdown or Quarto** document
alongside descriptive text. It dramatically improves the ability of someone
else to *understand* your archived code (transparency) and to *run* it
(functionality and reproducibility).
:::

Annotation is the letter with no direct FAIR equivalent, and the one most often
skipped. It is also the cheapest: it costs minutes while you are writing, and
hours if you leave it to the end.

## Annotate chunks, not lines {#annotated-chunks}

The recommendation is explicit: **annotate code chunks rather than every line
of code.** Line-by-line annotation is possible, but simply denoting and
describing relevant code chunks in sufficient detail is usually more helpful
for tracking what code does and what it produces.

A good chunk comment answers three questions:

1. **What** is this chunk doing? — *"Run a Poisson generalised linear model…"*
2. **Why** is it needed? — *"…to analyse caterpillar abundance varying with
   habitat…"*
3. **Where** does its output appear? — *"Numeric results shown in Caterpillar
   Abundance section"*, or *"Figure 5A"*

That third question is **signposting**, and it is the part people leave out. It
is what lets a reader — or a data editor, or a reviewer — connect a number in
your results section to the lines of code that produced it.

::: {.tada-compare}
::: {.tada-before}
Before

```r
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)
plot(dat$habitat, dat$n)
```

Nothing tells a reader what is being run, why it is being run, or what it
produces. There is no signposting at all.
:::

::: {.tada-after}
After

```r
##### Caterpillar abundance model #####
# Poisson GLM of caterpillar counts against habitat type, controlling
# for year, to test H1 (abundance differs between woodland types).
# Produces the coefficients reported in Table 2 and the numbers quoted
# in Results, "Caterpillar abundance".
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)

##### Figure 3A #####
# Raw counts by habitat, plotted as the left panel of Figure 3.
plot(dat$habitat, dat$n)
```
:::
:::

## Collapsible sections {#annotated-sections}

A small trick that pays off in long scripts. Certain comment markers create
**collapsible sections** in the editor, which increases readability and
facilitates structuring:

- **`#####`** in RStudio
- **`#%%`** in Python

```r
##### 1. Load and clean data #####
# ...

##### 2. Fit models #####
# ...

##### 3. Figures #####
# ...
```

In RStudio these appear in the document outline, so a reader can navigate a
600-line script from a sidebar instead of scrolling.

## Literate alternatives {#annotated-literate}

Rather than commenting a plain script, you can **embed the code within a
document alongside descriptive text**. The TADA guidelines list this as an
equally valid route to being annotated.

::: {.tabset}

### RMarkdown / Quarto {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Prose and code chunks in one file, with the output rendered inline. The
narrative *is* the annotation, and the link between a paragraph of explanation
and the code that follows it is unambiguous.

````markdown
## Caterpillar abundance

We fitted a Poisson GLM of counts against habitat type, controlling for
year, to test whether abundance differs between woodland types. These
coefficients are reported in Table 2.

```{r abundance-model}
m1 <- glm(n ~ habitat + year, family = poisson, data = dat)
summary(m1)
```
````

There is a further advantage the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) highlight:
presenting everything in one self-contained Markdown or Quarto document is
**very helpful for data editors and future readers**, because it makes the link
between the code, the data, and the resulting outputs explicit.

A rendered `.html` or `.pdf` of your Quarto document is a useful *addition* to
the archive — but archive the `.qmd`/`.Rmd` source too. A rendered PDF on its
own fails [Transferable](#transferable).

### Jupyter Notebook {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Notebooks (and JupyterLab) present code in chunks with descriptive text and
inline output, and are listed in TADA as an alternative route to annotated
code.

Two practical cautions when archiving one:

- **Restart and run all before you archive.** A notebook whose cells were run
  out of order records state that nobody can reproduce.
- **Notebooks store output in the file.** That is useful for readers, but means
  the archived `.ipynb` can be large and awkward to diff. Consider archiving
  both the notebook and a plain `.py` export.

### Plain scripts {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Nothing is wrong with a well-commented `.R` or `.py` file, and for many
analyses it is the clearest option. The requirements are the same:

- logical chunks, marked with `#####` / `#%%`
- a comment on each chunk giving what, why, and where the output appears
- object names that a reader can follow

If the analysis is long, split it across numbered scripts (`01_`, `02_`, `03_`)
and describe the order in the [README](#documented-readme).

:::

## Readability, briefly {#annotated-readability}

Annotation works best on code that is already legible. Four quick wins,
identified in the code review paper as ways to make code reviewable:

1. **Call packages explicitly** via the namespace — `package::function()` in R,
   `package.module.function()` in Python — so a reader knows where a function
   came from.
2. **Use relative file paths** (see [Transferable](#transferable-paths)).
3. **Remove redundant packages** — every `library()` call that is not needed is
   a dependency someone else has to install.
4. **Write analysis code with clear subheadings, intuitive comments and
   easy-to-understand object names.**

Formatters can enforce a consistent style with a single command: **`styler`**
(Müller & Walthert 2020) in R, **`pycodestyle`** (Rocholl 2022) in Python. Both
can format code to standardised styles — Google, tidyverse in R, or PEP 8 in
Python.

::: {.tada-note}
Style is not the same as annotation. A perfectly formatted script with no
comments still fails the Annotated test — and a slightly untidy script with
good chunk comments and signposting passes it. Do the comments first.
:::

## Do it as you go {#annotated-asyougo}

The SORTEE guidelines make the point plainly: annotating code as you produce
it — not only with section descriptions but also with information about how the
code runs and what output it produces — is **far easier than going back and
annotating at the end of the study**. The same applies to the README: create it
at the start and update it as files are added.

This is not just about effort. Annotation written six months after the fact is
reconstructed from memory, and reconstructed memory is where the errors hide.

## Checklist {#annotated-checklist}

- [ ] Code is broken into logical, labelled chunks
- [ ] Each chunk states what it does
- [ ] Each chunk states why it is needed
- [ ] Chunks that produce results signpost the manuscript location (figure, table, section)
- [ ] Collapsible section markers (`#####` / `#%%`) are used in long scripts
- [ ] Object names are interpretable by someone who did not write the code
- [ ] Packages are called explicitly by namespace where it aids clarity
- [ ] Unused `library()` / `import` calls have been removed
- [ ] If using a notebook: restarted and run top to bottom before archiving
- [ ] If using Quarto/RMarkdown: the **source** file is archived, not only the rendered output
